title: Jobs_2026 healthcare study
text:
The user selected healthcare data analysts in NAICS 62 and explicitly authorized local computation instead of the course’s assigned EC2 environment. Results below were generated from the local Jobs_2026 snapshot on October 3, 2026.
The pipeline read 2,350,355 rows in 97 posting partitions and selected January–September 2026 observations. All input files have recorded SHA-256 hashes. No posting ID appeared twice in this input snapshot.
Unknown country and unknown sector are exclusions, not negative industry labels. Staffing status that is missing is retained. The geographic and sector filters remove much of the source data, so the retained sample is not representative of all Jobs_2026 records or all US hiring.

These metrics measure agreement with dataset-derived sector labels, not independently verified employer truth. The GBDT misses 17 of the 35 healthcare employers while predicting no false positives among 38 other employers in this holdout. That small sample cannot establish perfect precision in deployment. The all-positive baseline has F1 0.648, close to GBDT’s 0.679; ranking models on F1 alone would conceal their very different precision and recall.
For a career product, predicted healthcare labels could narrow an employer-review queue, but the missed healthcare employers would make automatic exclusion costly. Retain existing labels and review disagreements before changing the career sample. No manually adjudicated undefined-employer labels are available, so the paper’s utility scores cannot be reproduced here.

title: Jobs_2026 healthcare study
text:
Training and feature details
Vocabulary thresholds are learned from the training employers only. The selected vocabulary contains 421 title candidates and 12 name words. After the 1% within-employer filter, the fitted matrix has 244 observed columns; candidates absent from all training feature vectors are dropped.
The linear SVM tests C = 0.1, 1 and 10 with balanced class penalties. GBDT tests depths 2 and 3 with 100 estimators and learning rate 0.1. Each model is chosen by validation F1, then evaluated on the test partition without refitting. Exact configurations, validation scores, versions and full classification reports are in run.json.

title: Jobs_2026 healthcare study
text:
Differences from the paper
This is an exploratory adaptation: a 2026 dataset, one industry, US-only observations, scikit-learn LinearSVC and GBDT, validation-based tuning instead of the paper’s reported cross-validation, and normalized employer-name unigrams without all raw name variants. Name-word frequency counts employers containing the word. The 80% dominant-sector rule is an explicit adaptation for inconsistent posting-level labels. A preliminary unrestricted-year, exact-consistency run exposed data-quality problems; its results are superseded. The final study is not a preregistered confirmatory replication.
Industry fields may themselves derive from title or employer heuristics. Their provenance has not been independently audited. Label circularity, unresolved aliases, cohort selection and noisy titles limit the meaning of predictive agreement. A temporal holdout and independent label review remain future validation work.

title: From postings to industry predictions
text:
For employer \(e\) and normalized title \(t\), let \(f_{e,t}\) be the posting frequency. The employer’s title share is
\[R_{e,t}=\frac{f_{e,t}}{\sum_{j\in T}f_{e,j}}, \qquad T_e=\{t:R_{e,t}\geq0.01\}.\]
For industry \(i\), the title significance score is
\[S_t^i=\frac{f_{t,p_i}}{f_t},\]
where the numerator is frequency among positive-class employers and the denominator is frequency across all employers. This score favors titles concentrated in the target industry. It is not a calibrated probability that an individual employer belongs to that industry.
The authors remove titles with \(f_{t,p_i}\leq1\), then use the medians of significance and frequency as selection thresholds. If the resulting vocabulary contains fewer than 50 titles, they lower the frequency threshold to its first quartile while retaining the significance threshold:
\[V_t^i=\{t:S_t^i\geq\theta_{s_i},\ f_t\geq\theta_{f_i}\}.\]
For a title in the selected vocabulary, the employer feature equals \(R_{e,t}\) when \(t\in T_e\), and zero otherwise. Source: Section III-A, equations 1–5.

title: From postings to industry predictions
text:
Models and imbalance
The paper uses LibSVM for SVM and Spark MLlib for GBDT. It reports cross-validation for hyperparameter selection but does not provide a complete search grid, random seed or final configuration. It describes cost-sensitive SVM training, with the positive-to-negative penalty ratio set according to the inverse class-size ratio:
\[\frac{C_{pos}}{C_{neg}}=\frac{N_{neg}}{N_{pos}}.\]
An exact kernel, tree depth or number of boosting iterations cannot be recovered from the supplied text. A modern implementation should document these choices as adaptations.

title: From postings to industry predictions
text:
Why disagreement matters
The authors collect employers for which model predictions disagree with legacy labels and review those records manually. Correctly identified entities are marked defined and assigned an industry label. Incorrectly computed entities are marked undefined. This distinction separates an industry-label error from a failure to identify the employer itself.
Disagreement review reduces the workload from 1,989 to 58 records for Transportation and from 1,991 to 217 for Health Care. A random audit of 100 agreement cases found 97 consistent with the assumed label. This audit supports selective review but also demonstrates that agreement is not a guarantee of correctness.

title: Employer industry classification using job postings
text:
Research question
Can the titles an employer hires for, together with words in its name, identify mistakes in its recorded industry? The study compares Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT). It distinguishes classification of valid employer entities from detection of incorrectly extracted or normalized employers.
The strongest practical result concerns error detection: GBDT has higher utility precision, recall and F-score than SVM for both industries. The existing knowledge-base system retains higher classification F-scores on defined employers. These are different evaluation tasks and should inform different deployment decisions.

text:
Scope and intended reader
This site is for students and analysts studying the reliability of job-market data. It reconstructs the supplied paper’s argument, equations and reported results, then adapts its approach to Jobs_2026. It does not rerun the original proprietary experiments. The authors of the underlying research are Mahak Goindani, Qiaoling Liu, Josh Chao and Valentin Jijkoun; the web reconstruction is AI-assisted and documented separately.
The paper studies Transportation and Warehousing and Health Care and Social Assistance. Their 2017 NAICS sectors are 48–49 and 62, respectively. The paper uses employer-level labels; the scope and unit of a course dataset must be checked before mapping its codes to these sectors.

title: Interpretation and limitations
text:
The study offers a way to prioritize records for inspection. A hiring profile can reveal that a name was parsed incorrectly, linked to the wrong company, or assigned the wrong knowledge-base attribute. The evidence supports a review workflow; it does not establish that automatically replacing legacy labels would improve overall classification.
The paper’s explanation for GBDT’s higher utility is that trees can capture relationships among related titles. This is a proposed explanation, not a controlled causal finding about why one model outperformed the other.

The evidence supports a review workflow; it does not establish that automatically replacing legacy labels would improve overall classification.

title: Interpretation and limitations
text:
When the main assumption fails
The approach assumes that frequent job titles reveal the employer’s principal industry. An employer hiring mostly support roles can violate that assumption. In the paper’s CGB Enterprises example, frequent non-core roles and an uninformative employer name lead the model away from the correct Transportation label.
Staffing agencies are another challenge: their vacancies may describe client industries. The authors report low precision and recall in an additional staffing experiment but do not provide numerical scores. Multi-industry companies also strain the single-main-industry assumption.

title: Interpretation and limitations
text:
Limits of evaluation
The training labels are noisy. Most agreement cases inherit a presumed-correct label rather than an independent adjudication. The 97-of-100 audit does not eliminate possible correlated errors shared by the model and legacy system. Results based on high-volume employers in one three-month period may differ for smaller employers, later periods or other sectors.
The unavailable original data, model settings and normalization resources limit exact replication. The inconsistent published sample counts add a further reconciliation requirement.

title: Interpretation and limitations
text:
Related work in the paper
CompanyDepot provides the employer-normalization context (Liu, Javed and McNair, 2016; Liu and colleagues, 2017). Carotene supplies the job-title-classification context (Javed and colleagues, 2015). Bernstein, Clearwater and Provost (2003) study industry classification through relational signals such as company co-occurrence. The present paper instead uses recruiting activity. These descriptions follow Section VI and the bibliography of the supplied paper; the underlying related-work publications have not been independently reviewed for this reconstruction.

title: Interpretation and limitations
text:
Extensions proposed by the authors
The paper suggests employer descriptions, job-description features, title entropy for staffing, and multiclass or multilabel prediction. These are future directions, not results established by the published experiments.

title: Data and preparation
text:
Preparation sequence

Link employer-name mentions to normalized employer entities.
Associate postings and normalized job titles with each entity.
Exclude employers with fewer than 20 postings when generating features.
Retain titles representing at least 1% of an employer’s postings.
Select industry-specific title and employer-name vocabularies.
Build employer-level feature vectors for separate binary tasks.

The paper describes random 70% training, 10% validation and 20% test partitions. Its starting title inventory contains 5,426 normalized titles. This is a specialized normalization resource, not simply lowercased raw titles.

title: Data and preparation
text:
Data availability and leakage controls
The supplied materials contain the paper, not the employer-level records, normalization system, knowledge base, fitted models or reviewed labels. An exact numerical replication is therefore unavailable from these materials alone.
For a new study, split by normalized employer before learning label-dependent vocabularies, and fit thresholds on training data only. Freeze vocabulary, label mapping and model selection before examining the test set. These are proposed replication controls; the paper does not fully document the fitting boundary for vocabulary selection.
For Jobs_2026, preserve a source manifest, schema, observation dates, duplicate rules, row counts after each filter, missingness and employer resolution decisions. Never infer that a title such as software engineer determines the employer’s industry.

title: Career evaluation logic
text: Industry classification helps determine whether a posting belongs in the selected analytical sample. It does not measure whether the job is desirable, accessible or well matched to a student. Records with disputed employer identity should enter a review queue before contributing to sector-level advice.

text:
Missingness and sensitivity
Do not rank a segment when a required component is missing. Report coverage and the reason for withholding its score. If all compared values for a dimension are equal, that dimension contains no ranking information; declare a neutral common score. Repeat rankings under equal weights and changes of ±10 percentage points to major weights, renormalizing to sum to 1. Report rank changes instead of presenting one weighting as objectively correct.

title: Career evaluation logic
text:
Evaluation for a new classifier
Use an employer-disjoint holdout and independently reviewed labels. Report precision, recall, F1, class support and a confusion matrix separately for each industry. Review a sample of both agreement and disagreement records. A fair comparison should include the legacy label system and simple baselines. Document how many review flags are useful and the analyst time required.
Current status: the Jobs_2026 study fits and evaluates a linear SVM and GBDT, including confusion matrices and simple baselines. It uses dataset-derived labels without independent adjudication. Market benchmarks have been calculated, but the weighted career scorecard remains uncomputed because personal ratings and sufficient salary evidence are unavailable. Classification is the completed Module 5 analytical track.

title: Healthcare analyst market baseline
text:
The selected career sample contains 112 postings dated 2026-01-15 through 2026-09-28. The scope is US healthcare data analysts in NAICS 62. Title matching includes data analyst, data analytics analyst, business intelligence analyst, BI analyst, clinical analyst and healthcare analyst phrases. Matching uses raw title, with clean title as fallback. This includes some clinical systems roles and can miss analyst titles phrased differently.
The benchmark uses the posting’s supplied industry label. It does not filter on a model prediction. These are observed dataset counts, not estimates of all open jobs or currently live vacancies. Expiration and active-URL status were not used to define the cohort.

title: Healthcare analyst market baseline
text:
Salary and experience limits
Only 3 observations have both explicit USD currency and a positive normalized salary amount. The website withholds a headline median because this is below an analyst-selected minimum of 10 comparable observations. Missing currency is not assumed to be USD. Normalization factors and extracted salary evidence were not independently reviewed, so even the retained values require validation before salary advice.
The median supplied minimum-experience value is 0, but zero values cannot establish that employers accept beginners. Review original requirement text before making accessibility recommendations. Raw job descriptions are intentionally not republished by this website.
Download the benchmark table, state counts, and work-arrangement counts. Reproduce them with the script and input hashes listed on the study page.

title: Recommendations
text:
Use model–legacy disagreement to prioritize employer-record review. Preserve the original label, proposed label, evidence and reviewer decision rather than silently overwriting the knowledge base. Distinguish name-extraction, entity-normalization and industry-attribute errors because their remedies differ.
Compare models against the actual operational objective. The paper favors GBDT for finding undefined employers, while the legacy system retains higher classification F-scores. An error-discovery model and a production labeler need not be the same system.
Audit agreement cases as well as flagged records. The paper’s 97-of-100 agreement audit leaves evidence of residual error. A new study should budget for independent review across both groups.

title: Recommendations
text:
For a student career product
The healthcare-analyst sample most often lists SQL: 63 of 112 postings (56.25%). Tableau appears in 36 (32.1%), while Power BI, Python and Excel each appear in 26 (23.2%). A learning portfolio centered on SQL and one visualization tool is a defensible starting point for this sample. These are market-frequency priorities, not findings that an individual lacks those skills or that acquiring them causes employment.
The sample includes 24 explicitly remote and 20 hybrid postings, but 58 have unknown work arrangement. Read each listing before treating it as a remote option. Virginia, New York and California have the largest known state counts, but 42 postings lack a usable state. These small, selected counts do not establish that relocating would improve career prospects.
Only three postings have explicit USD currency and a positive normalized salary. Withhold a salary recommendation. A supplied minimum-experience value of zero may mean unspecified requirements; do not treat the 44 records with values from zero to two as verified entry-level opportunities.

title: Recommendations

Review a sample of employer labels and raw requirement text, resolve suspected aliases, and collect participant ratings if personal skill-gap analysis is needed. GBDT misses 17 of 35 healthcare employers in the holdout, so automatic exclusion based on its predictions would omit relevant opportunities. Use model disagreement for review. Repeat in the assigned EC2 environment if submitting under the unmodified course rules.

Reproduce the Jobs_2026 adaptation

Replace the data-directory argument with your authorized copy. The script reads only jobs_2026_part_*.parquet; the salary-options lookup is not a posting partition. It scans all 97 parts, streams selected columns, and records hashes, filters, versions, settings and metrics in run.json. Source postings and descriptions are not redistributed. Aggregates live in data/study/; charts live in images/.
The period is January 1 through September 30, 2026. The script keeps the first occurrence of each posting ID in filename order. Different IDs for the same real vacancy are not resolved. Country must be explicitly US, industry must be present, and explicitly flagged staffing records are excluded. The dominant employer sector must cover at least 80% of its eligible postings. See the study for adaptations and limitations.

title: Skill-gap analysis
text:
Personal assessment evidence
Module 3 asks each team member to rate relevant skills from 1 (beginner) to 5 (advanced), then compare those profiles with market requirements. Market frequencies have now been computed, but no participant profiles have been supplied. Individual gaps and career-readiness scores cannot be inferred from market frequencies.

title: Skill-gap analysis
text:
Proposed calculation
After extracting the selected pathway’s skills, let \(w_s\) be the fraction of postings requesting skill \(s\). Let \(r_s\) be a documented target proficiency and \(p_{u,s}\) a person’s self-reported proficiency on the course’s 1–5 scale. Define
\[g_{u,s}=\max(0,r_s-p_{u,s}), \qquad priority_{u,s}=w_sg_{u,s}.\]
This is a proposed course scorecard, not a method from the paper. Posting frequency alone does not establish required proficiency. Set targets using explicit job requirements or an explained rubric, and retain the source for each target. Missing self-ratings remain unknown rather than being replaced with 1.
